posts.text: Agentic AI, explained on one whiteboard. Most people use "agents" as a buzzword. The board breaks it into 5 levels, and each level contains everything to its left. Level 1 is traditional machine learning. Learning patterns from data to make predictions, like a model that prices houses. Level 2 is enhanced ML. Same models, better results, through feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, cross-validation, and ensembles. Level 3 is intelligent applications. Models deployed in real products with context and feedback. Real-time inference, data pipelines, monitoring, A/B testing. Think recommendation systems. Level 4 is autonomous agents. Systems that make decisions and act with limited human intervention. The core loop is perceive, decide, act, backed by goal setting, memory, and environment interaction. An auto-trading bot lives here. Level 5 is agentic systems. Fully autonomous systems that plan, learn, and pursue complex goals across domains. The loop upgrades to plan, execute, reflect, learn. Strategic planning, multi-step reasoning, tool use, self-improvement. An AI research assistant is the canonical example. Two things apply at every level. The principles nobody gets to skip. Safety, ethics, privacy, transparency, human in the loop. And the enablers nobody gets to skip either. Data quality, compute, MLOps, evals, and the talent to run it all. Success is simple to define. The system solves real problems, adapts to change, creates value, improves over time, and stays aligned with human goals. posts.text: +80.8%, then -70%. I used to think more agents meant an upgrade. But then I found this research. A controlled study tested 260 configurations, across 6 benchmarks and 5 architectures. On the right kind of task, multi-agent improved performance by 80.8%. On the wrong kind, it killed performance by 70%. And the difference wasn't coming from the technology. But whether the task could actually be split up, or not. There is something even more interesting. When agents work independently, with nobody checking their output, errors got amplified 17.2x. Add just one check of their work and that dropped to 4.4x. Just because someone started checking. The cost side problem is also serious. Anthropic: A single agent uses about 4x the tokens of a normal chat. A multi-agent system uses about 15x. Run that at 10,000 tasks a month, and the gap is hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. I don't want to scare you. Or to make you think that you should never use more than one agent. It is just not always that easy to choose if you need one or many. I've found a study where a multi-agent system was 94% cheaper than a single agent. And even more accurate. It used cheaper models for the easy parts, instead of running everything through the expensive one. That's why your choice between one or many should be economic, not aesthetic. Don't make the decision based on instinct. So I put together 7 mistakes that cause this decision to go wrong. Don't make them like most and you will save a ton. posts.text: Agentic AI is not a tool upgrade. It is a shift in how work gets done. At a high level, this image points to systems that plan, act, observe, and adapt on their own. That matters because most professional workflows were designed for static software and manual oversight. Those assumptions break when intelligence becomes continuous instead of transactional. For teams, the real problem agentic AI solves is not speed. It is coordination under complexity. When tasks span tools, time, memory, and changing constraints, humans end up stitching decisions together by hand. That is slow, error prone, and mentally expensive. Applied well, agentic systems change the unit of work. You stop thinking in individual prompts or features. You start designing goals, boundaries, and feedback loops. What improves is not just output quality. Decision latency drops. Context stops leaking between steps. Failures become visible earlier and easier to correct. Workflows gain the ability to recover instead of collapse. Practically, this means a few things for professionals right now. Design work as a sequence of decisions, not actions. Separate memory from reasoning so systems can learn without drifting. Use tools as extensions of intent, not hardcoded steps. Build in observation so every run teaches the next one something useful. Treat orchestration and evaluation as first class work, not afterthoughts. The biggest mindset shift is this. You are no longer operating software. You are shaping behavior over time. Once you see that clearly, the way you design systems, teams, and even your own role starts to change. ---------------------------------------------------- Learn AI in 3 Minutes a Day 👉 https://lnkd.in/gD9SfU5J ----------------------------------------------------

posts.text: When we build multi-agent systems, we divide work into roles. One agent researches, another analyzes, another checks the result. We define their tools and how they exchange information, then expect to replace or upgrade each component without redesigning the whole system. Adding persistent memory complicates that assumption. Agents can retain procedures and lessons from earlier tasks, including expectations about how their teammates behave. Over time, some of what makes an agent effective may depend on the particular team it has worked with. An interesting paper I came across, “Testing Interchangeability in LLM Agent Teams,” investigates this through a controlled swap experiment. The researchers formed eight independent teams per setting. Agents shared the same base model and role prompts, but kept private notebooks across ten episodes together. They then swapped equally experienced agents with matching roles between teams and evaluated the new pairings on held-out tasks. A control announced a replacement but returned the original agent. Task scores changed little, but communication per unit of progress increased by 16–63%. In Hanabi, an experienced agent from another team required more signalling effort than an inexperienced replacement. Longer shared histories increased the swap penalty in the tested conditions. The notebooks contained expectations about who acts without being asked, who needs explicit instructions, what signals mean and when handoffs happen. These habits were stored in text; model weights stayed unchanged. Consider an illustrative research-and-analysis workflow. The researcher learns that its partner checks missing citations automatically, so it stops explicitly flagging them. The analyst learns that an empty field means “still being investigated,” rather than “nothing found.” An equally capable replacement may interpret those signals differently. The tools still connect and the messages still arrive, but the assumptions behind them no longer match. Additional clarification and corrections may preserve the final result while making the workflow more expensive. For builders, the distinction is between knowing how to perform a role and knowing how to perform it with a particular partner. Matching the model, instructions and tools may preserve the first without preserving the second. I would therefore test replacements after a team has accumulated experience, measuring communication and execution cost alongside completion. Evaluating each agent independently, or testing only fresh teams, could miss dependencies that emerge through memory. A design implication worth testing is to separate reusable task knowledge from partner-specific expectations. A procedure for validating a record should transfer between teams. An assumption that another agent always performs that validation needs checking when membership changes. Paper: https://lnkd.in/ejWVnGhT

commentSamples.text: The key distinction here is simple: a failed response is not the same as a failed action. That one assumption changes how you design retries.
This is the kind of failure that rarely shows up in demos. Production reliability is usually about the workflow around the model, not the model itself.
Idempotency helps, but verification is what gives the agent a way to reason about what actually happened before acting again.
Managing idempotency keys and post-action verification states properly prevents double execution when API timeouts occur.
Harish Agoram Exactly. Idempotency protects the action, and post-action verification restores certainty. You really need both if retries are going to be safe.
This is where agent reliability gets interesting. A correct decision is not enough if the system cannot distinguish failure from an unknown state before retrying.

posts.text: The most expensive AI agent bug can happen after the agent makes the correct decision. It chooses the right tool. Passes the right arguments. Executes the right action. Then the response times out. Now the dangerous part starts. The agent has to decide: Did the action fail? Or did the action succeed and only the confirmation fail? If your workflow treats both as the same thing, the obvious recovery is: retry. That sounds safe. Until the action was: issuing a refund, sending an invoice, creating an order, updating a CRM record, or emailing a customer. Now “retry” can mean “do it twice.” This is why production agent reliability cannot stop at: Did the model choose the correct tool? You also need to design what happens after the tool call. For every action that changes state, I’d map: What proves the action succeeded? Can the agent check that state? Can the same action safely run twice? When should it retry? When should it stop? When should it escalate? That usually means combining idempotency, post-action verification, retry rules, and a clear unknown-state path. The LLM might make the right decision. But the workflow still has to survive an unreliable network, API timeout, or partial failure. That’s the difference between an agent that can call tools… and an agent you can trust to operate a business workflow.

posts.text: What if the next enterprise AI problem isn’t adoption, but sprawl? Over the last few years, the focus has been on getting organizations to experiment with AI. Now many are facing a different challenge. Copilots. Agents. Pilots. Vendors. Business-led solutions. Different teams solving similar problems in different ways. Individually, many of these investments may make sense. Collectively, leadership can lose sight of: What do we actually have? What is creating value? What overlaps? What should scale? And what should we stop? I think the next phase of enterprise AI will require as much discipline around portfolio strategy and rationalization as it does experimentation. Moving fast still matters. But so does knowing whether everyone is moving in the same direction. At what point does AI experimentation become AI sprawl? Strong distinction between formal exception authority and informal override. The next governance question is therefore very practical: When an exception expires or its reassessment condition is triggered, what mechanism makes the superseded exception non-consumable before the next consequential execution? That is where policy intent has to become operationally enforceable. An exception is a bounded warrant, not an unconditional continuation right. …more

posts.text: 🚨 The hardest AI governance decision often starts after governance says “no.” The system works. The business case is strong. The executive sponsor wants it live. But governance identifies a material risk that can’t be fully mitigated. 🛑 Privacy says no. 🛑 Security isn’t comfortable. 🛑 Legal sees unresolved exposure. 🛑 The controls don’t reduce the risk enough. Does that automatically mean the initiative should die? Not necessarily. But proceeding can’t mean an executive simply says, “Do it anyway.” That’s not risk acceptance. That’s an undocumented override. A mature AI governance model needs a formal exception process that answers: 📌 What requirement is being overridden? ⚠️ What residual risk remains? 💡 Why is proceeding justified? 👤 Who is formally accepting the risk? 🔒 What conditions or restrictions apply? ⏰ When does the exception expire? 🔄 What would trigger reassessment? The problem isn’t exceptions. The problem is uncontrolled exceptions. And there’s a broader governance principle here: The authority required to accept AI risk should increase with the materiality of that risk. Governance teams shouldn’t be forced to make enterprise risk decisions beyond their authority. Business leaders shouldn’t be able to quietly override governance without assuming accountability. This is a post in my latest series: 🔥 When AI Governance Meets Reality I’m looking at the messy situations where clean governance frameworks collide with business pressure, competing priorities, ambiguity, and real-world accountability. 💬 If your AI governance team recommended against deploying a high-value AI system, but the business wanted to proceed anyway: Who would actually have the final decision and would that person formally own the risk? hashtag #AIGovernance hashtag #ArtificialIntelligence hashtag #RiskManagement hashtag #ResponsibleAI hashtag #EnterpriseAI hashtag #AICompliance hashtag #Governance

posts.text: In multi-agent synthesis, summarisation is a lossy transformation. Unless attribution is bound to each claim at extraction, every downstream hop silently strips the metadata that made the output defensible — and no later agent can reconstruct it. The architecture treats provenance as a data contract rather than a citation style. Extraction emits one record per atomic claim, carrying source, document locator, verbatim excerpt, publication and retrieval timestamps, confidence and caveats. Very importantly, Synthesis agents should merge record sets by reference; natural language is rendered only at the terminal surface. Where credible sources disagree, both values persist with their own attribution — and timestamps distinguish genuine change over time from contradiction. Enforce these invariants in code at the hop boundary, not in the system prompt: structural constraints survive compression, instructions do not. Every figure a board or regulator sees then resolves deterministically to a document, a passage and a date.

posts.text: Five banks. Five approaches to AI. And five very different ways of showing that it is creating value. As we get closer to the HFS banking roundtable in Toronto on Oct 8, I’ve been spending a lot of time looking at how Canada’s banks are moving AI from pilots into production. The discussion will be led by Phil Fersht alongside Arindam Mukhopadhyay and Melissa Fersht, in collaboration with Infosys. We’ll have just 20 senior banking and financial-services leaders around the table under Chatham House rules. So, as part of my homework for Toronto, I wanted to put Canada’s Big 5 side by side. The infographic gives you the snapshot. What I find particularly interesting is what the CEOs are saying and where AI is actually starting to show up in the business. 🔹 RBC | Dave McKay: “AI is a generational technology that has the power to reimagine what’s possible for our business.” RBC is targeting C$700m-C$1bn in AI-driven enterprise value by 2027. Some of its strongest publicly documented activity spans capital markets, retail credit and wealth — including AidenBanker, ATOM and RBC Assist. 🔹 TD | Raymond Chunn: talks about the opportunity to “power our businesses with AI.” TD has set out medium-term ambitions of C$500m in annualized revenue uplift and C$500m in annualized savings. Retail lending, branches/contact centres and insurance are particularly interesting areas to watch. 🔹 Scotiabank | Scott Thomson: has talked about using AI to “simplify, digitize, and streamline the way we do business.” Scotia Intelligence provides the enterprise foundation, while we're seeing tangible applications across digital banking, commercial banking and payments — including a reported 70% reduction in manual work in commercial email processing. 🔹 BMO | Darryl White: talks about a “human- and AI-powered” approach to CX. Some of BMO’s clearest publicly documented activity is in Personal & Business Banking and Insurance. Lumi has delivered a reported 17% productivity improvement among new employees, alongside applications in personalization and underwriting. 🔹 CIBC | Harry Culham: says the bank is using AI to enable its teams to “do more for our clients.” CIBC is particularly interesting as it moves from assistants towards agents. CAI is available to more than 50,000 employees, while DocuMind is reported to save an average of 16,000 hours per quarter. What strikes me looking across all five is that AI value doesn’t have one definition. Revenue. Cost. Hours released. Productivity. Faster decisions. Better client experiences. The real challenge is connecting those individual measures to sustainable enterprise value and understanding what has to change in technology, data, governance, processes and operating models to get there. That’s exactly the conversation I’m looking forward to hearing around the table in Toronto. hashtag #Banking hashtag #AI hashtag #FinancialServices hashtag #Canada hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #HFSResearch

posts.text: Most teams jump straight to Agentic AI frameworks. Then wonder why their agent works in demos but breaks in production. The framework isn’t the foundation. Here’s the stack you need to understand: 1. Core Principles Agents are: → Goal-driven → Autonomous → Able to perceive and reason → Capable of taking actions through tools → Able to adapt from outcomes and feedback 2. The Agent Loop Perceive → Reason → Plan → Act → Memory → Observe → Repeat Every weak link in this loop creates unreliable behavior. 3. Agent Types → Simple Reflex - rule-based responses → Goal-Based - works toward defined objectives → Utility-Based - chooses the best action → Learning Agent - improves through feedback → Multi-Agent - multiple agents working together 4. The Core Stack • LLM = Brain • Tools = Hands • Memory = Context • Knowledge = Information • Guardrails = Control 5. Building an Agent Define goal → Design workflow → Choose tools → Add memory → Add guardrails → Test → Deploy & monitor 6. Tools Orchestration: LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI Vector DBs: Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant Observability: LangSmith, Arize, W&B Deployment: Docker, Kubernetes, Modal 7. Measure What Matters • Task success • Accuracy • Cost & speed • Reliability • User satisfaction Treating Agentic AI like a framework problem. Master the principles first. Then choose the tools. posts.text: 🛑 Here’s the part of enterprise AI people often underestimate: the model is only one piece of the system. 👉 You can pick the best model available and still end up with something that is difficult to trust, expensive to run, or impossible to govern. Because production AI needs a lot more around it. You need reliable data sources and integration. You need governance so the system knows what data it can use, who owns it, and how sensitive information should be handled. You need retrieval so the AI can work with trusted enterprise context instead of guessing. ‼️ Then come the layers that make the system actually usable: → Model selection → AI gateways → Agent orchestration → Enterprise integrations → Guardrails and security → Human approvals → Monitoring and observability → Lifecycle management And this is where things get interesting. The model may generate the answer. 👉 But the rest of the stack decides: ✅ Can it access the right information? ✅ Can it take action safely? ✅ Can someone audit what happened? ✅ Can it recover when something fails? ✅ Can you control cost and latency? ✅ Can you improve it over time? That is the difference between an AI demo and an AI system you can actually depend on. I think teams will spend a lot more time designing these surrounding layers over the next few years than debating which model is “best.” ❓ Which layer do you think gets ignored most often in enterprise AI projects? Credit to Matthew Coombs. Follow him for more.

posts.text: In companies’ rush to capitalize on artificial intelligence, ethics and governance considerations often take a back seat. That’s a concern, said Jeffrey Saviano, an MIT Sloan senior lecturer with three decades of experience at EY. When applied together, AI ethics and responsible governance can help ensure that AI systems are safe, fair, and aligned with human, organizational, and societal values. Companies that fail to address these complex issues “won’t know how to respond when faced with a real AI-related problem,” Saviano said in a recent presentation. Saviano estimated that ethics and governance practices lag AI adoption by at least a couple of years. “Execs see the potential AI can have on organizations, and it’s creating a chaotic frenzy to quickly launch new solutions,” he said. Saviano and his research team developed a framework to help organizations assess their position on the AI ethics maturity spectrum. Among their recommended best practices: • Create a board-level technology committee with formal responsibility for the governance and oversight of AI systems. • Make AI ethics and governance a cross-functional effort. Learn more: https://lnkd.in/gnQDi-Cf
